declared.title: The Matthew effect in science funding
declared.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
declared.foundIn: Crossref search « The Matthew effect in science funding Bol de Vaan van de Rijt » (2026-11-26); named by the counter-evidence review

population: early-career researchers in the Netherlands (NWO « Veni » grants): applicants just above vs just below the funding threshold, followed 8 to 16 years

findings.text: Those who narrowly missed an early grant gathered less than half the research funding of narrow winners over the next eight years, not counting the early grant itself

support.sentence: Analyses of review scores reveal that early funding success introduces a growing rift, with winners just above the funding threshold accumulating more than twice as much research funding (€180,000) during the following eight years as nonwinners just below it.

findings.text: Part of the gap came from those who narrowly failed: they applied for another grant less often

support.sentence: Surprisingly, however, the emergent funding gap is partly created by applicants, who, after failing to win one grant, apply for another grant less often.

limits: quasi-experiment (regression discontinuity around the funding threshold, mostly ranks ±1/±2), not random assignment; `longitudinal` for lack of a quasi-experiment value
the outcome is later funding and posts, partly a gatekeeping effect of the first grant (reviewers favour past winners), not what the failure taught
full text: no discontinuity at the threshold in publications, citations or h-index, before or after: the near miss left the work itself neither better nor worse
full text: the €180,000 gap excludes the €250,000 grant itself; full professor 10-16 years later 19% vs 28%; applying again 40% vs 59%, not from leaving academia or the country
one programme, one country, early-career researchers; number of applicants near the threshold in the SI appendix, not read (anti-robot page)
Traag et al. 2025 (eLife reviewed preprint, a replication) finds the Matthew effect robust across funders
